newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia wage ruling to set commission role.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia wage ruling to set commission role.

text.p: Unions hope Australia's chief industrial tribunal will entrench its authority under the government's decentralised wages system by granting broad pay rises when it decides a major wage claim in the next few weeks.

Australia's conservative government, extending the reforms of its Labor predecessor, changed the system last year to further emphasise workplace bargaining rather than the old administered "award" wages set centrally by the Industrial Relations Commission.

With private bargaining as an alternative, general rises in awards are no longer necessary but the commission is considering a union application, opposed by the government, to boost the lower pay scales of awards.

"What the commission does will really determine its relevance and role in the future and we're hoping it will take a positive role so we don't get a large growth of people who are working full-time, but are essentially under the poverty line," an Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) spokesman, who declined to be named, told Reuters.

A senior politics lecturer at the Australian National University, Gwen Gray, said the decision on the direction of wages for the next three years would indicate how central the commission's role would be under the conservative government.
"If it does what the government wants or even if it comes down with some sort of half-way agreement, I would say it's pretty much bowing to government pressure," Gray told Reuters.

The government and the central bank, the Reserve Bank of Australia, have both called for the commission to be conservative in setting wages, warning that a wages blow-out would pose a serious threat to Australia's low inflation rate.
The government has also warned that the ACTU's claim could lead to fewer jobs.
Gray said it was difficult to predict what action the government was likely to take if the commission decided to approve the ACTU's so-called "living wage" claim.
Any action to further reduce its powers was likely to be stymied in the upper house of parliament, the Senate, where the government does not have a majority, she said.

"But to rein in the powers of the arbitration commission, that would require some sort of legislation and it's unlikely that the Democrats (a Left-leaning minor party) would allow that to go through the Senate."
A spokesman for Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith doubted the commission's decision was likely to give an indication of its future role.
"The commission has heard the submissions and it will decide the issue on the merits of the case," the spokesman said.
"For the ACTU to say unless they sign up to absolutely everything they say, that's absolutely ridiculous. It's quite a ridiculous proposition."
The government has proposed a A$24 a week safety net adjustment -- given to help people unable to privately negotiate a pay rise with their employers -- spread over three years.
The ACTU has called for an 8.75 percent increase in award rates for all workers not covered by workplace agreements, plus three A$20 a week safety net adjustments over three years.
